reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Approach the burned patient as a trauma patient first, following the primary survey, because associated injuries and airway compromise can be immediately lethal
Assess the airway early: facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth, hoarseness, and stridor warn of inhalational injury and the need for early intubation before oedema closes the airway
Estimate burn size using validated methods (rule of nines or a palm-based estimate) counting only partial- and full-thickness burns
Burn depth guides prognosis: superficial burns blanch and are painful, whereas full-thickness burns are leathery, insensate, and non-blanching
Large burns require fluid resuscitation titrated to urine output using a body-surface-area and weight-based formula as a starting estimate
Circumferential full-thickness burns of a limb or the chest can cause a compartment or ventilatory crisis requiring escharotomy
Suspect carbon monoxide or cyanide toxicity in enclosed-space fires, since pulse oximetry can read falsely normal
Keep the patient warm and provide adequate analgesia, as burns cause rapid heat and fluid loss and severe pain
reference.pathophysiology: Heat denatures proteins and causes coagulative necrosis of skin, with a central zone of coagulation surrounded by zones of stasis and hyperaemia that can progress to necrosis if perfusion falls. Loss of the skin barrier and a systemic inflammatory response increase capillary permeability, causing large fluid shifts, intravascular volume depletion, and burn shock in extensive injuries. Inhalational injury combines direct thermal damage to the upper airway, chemical injury to the lower airways from combustion products, and systemic asphyxiants such as carbon monoxide and cyanide. Later, the denuded surface predisposes to infection and hypermetabolism.
additionalDifferentials: Chemical or electrical burns with different management priorities
Scald injury versus non-accidental injury patterns
Toxic epidermal necrolysis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome mimicking a burn
Cold injury (frostbite) in the differential of tissue necrosis
additionalInvestigations: Carboxyhaemoglobin level and arterial blood gas where inhalation is suspected
Serial urine output monitoring to titrate fluid resuscitation
Baseline bloods including electrolytes, renal function, and haematocrit
Bronchoscopy to assess and confirm inhalational airway injury in selected cases
Serial examination of circumferential burns for compartment compromise
redFlags: Signs of inhalational injury (hoarseness, stridor, soot, facial burns) demanding early airway control before oedema progresses
Extensive burns with evolving hypovolaemic shock requiring aggressive titrated resuscitation
Circumferential full-thickness burns threatening limb perfusion or ventilation and needing escharotomy
Suspected carbon monoxide or cyanide poisoning from an enclosed-space fire
Rapidly rising resuscitation fluid requirements or falling urine output indicating under-resuscitation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on burn size and depth, age, inhalational injury, and comorbidity. Small partial-thickness burns heal well, whereas large or full-thickness burns and inhalational injury carry higher mortality and long-term morbidity, including scarring and functional loss.
pitfalls: Delaying airway assessment until oedema makes intubation difficult or impossible
Under- or over-estimating burn area, leading to incorrect fluid resuscitation
Relying on pulse oximetry, which can appear normal in carbon monoxide poisoning
Missing associated trauma by focusing only on the visible burn
Allowing hypothermia during exposure and fluid administration
management: Manage as trauma with a primary survey and secure the airway early — intubating before oedema develops — when inhalational injury is suspected
Resuscitate large burns with warmed crystalloid titrated to urine output using a body-surface-area and weight-based formula as the starting estimate
Treat systemic asphyxiants: high-flow oxygen for carbon monoxide and hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide toxicity
Provide burn wound care with cleaning, topical antimicrobials and dressings, and early tangential excision with skin grafting for deep partial- and full-thickness burns
Perform escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness burns causing limb ischaemia or ventilatory compromise
Give adequate analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, early high-protein nutritional support for the hypermetabolic response, and vigilance for wound infection
Refer major burns to a specialist burns centre for multidisciplinary care, rehabilitation and scar management
